s: Ormuzd, also called Oromasdes by the Greeks, remained faithful to the supreme being who created him and became the source of all good. He created man and supplied the materials of happiness, and his followers are expected eventually to triumph over Ahriman and his followers.

l: Ahriman, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter XXX
s: Ahriman, also called Arimanes, rebelled against the supreme creator and became the author of evil. He marred human happiness by introducing evil into the world and creating savage beasts, poisonous reptiles, and harmful plants; he is ultimately destined to be consigned to darkness.

l: good and evil, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter XXX
s: In Zoroastrian teaching, good and evil are mingled throughout the present world, and their adherents wage continual war. The text states that good will eventually be victorious and that evil will be confined to darkness forever.

l: Persia, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter XXX
s: Persia was the center of the religion of Zoroaster, which dominated Western Asia from the time of Cyrus to Alexander the Great and later regained influence after corruption under the Macedonian monarchy. The Arab conquest in the seventh century caused many Persians to abandon the ancient faith, while others fled to Kerman and Hindustan.

l: Parsees, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter XXX
s: The Parsees are Persians who refused to abandon their ancestral religion and fled to Kerman and Hindustan after the Arab conquest. They remained especially numerous at Bombay, where the text describes them as active, intelligent, wealthy, honest, pure in life, and conciliatory in manner.

l: Vedas, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter XXX
s: The Vedas are the sacred books on which Hindu religion is professedly founded, and Hindus attribute their composition to Brahma at the creation. The present arrangement is attributed to Vyasa, and the Vedas are said to contain the rules of faith and religious ceremonies.

l: Brahma, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter XXX
s: Brahma is presented as the supreme God, creator of the universe, and source into which all individual deities and human souls will ultimately be absorbed. As the creator in the Trimurti, Brahma later became associated with the priestly class, but his worship eventually disappeared and he was left with only one temple in India.

l: Vishnu, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter XXX
s: Vishnu is the preserving principle in the Hindu triad and protects the world through successive incarnations. His most celebrated human form is Krishna, and his tenth Avatar, Kalki, is expected to destroy vice and restore virtue at the end of the present age.

l: Siva, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter XXX
s: Siva is the third person of the Hindu triad and represents destruction, though in the Puranas he is more particularly associated with regeneration. He has more worshippers and a wider worship than Brahma, and his followers form one of the two major Hindu sects.

l: Trimurti, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter XXX
s: The Trimurti unites Brahma, Vishnu, and Siva as the three personified powers of creation, preservation, and destruction. The text describes it as a Brahmanical compromise intended to unite different classes of worshippers against the Buddhists.

l: Krishna, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter XXX
s: Krishna is the human form in which Vishnu appeared as an invincible warrior. Through his exploits he relieved the earth from tyrants who oppressed it, and passages praising him were inserted into the Mahabharata.

l: Avatars of Vishnu, Bulfinch's Mythology: The Age of Fable, Chapter XXX
s: The Avatars of Vishnu are bodily forms in which Vishnu descends to earth to protect the world during times of danger. The text identifies ten especially important Avatars, including Matsya, the Fish, who preserved Manu during a universal deluge, the Tortoise, and Krishna; Kalki is the tenth.
